text:
Education in Poland is a state-regulated system with compulsory education ending at age 18, following a structure of eight years of primary school ( *szkoła podstawowa* ), three years of junior high school ( *gimnazjum* ), and three years of upper secondary school ( *liceum* ). A major 2017 reform reverted the system to an 8+3+3 structure, abolishing the previous 6+3+3 model and extending primary education to ensure core subjects are taught earlier. The upper secondary phase offers general education ( *liceum* ), leading to the *Matura* qualification required for university entry, as well as vocational tracks including technical schools ( *technikum* ) lasting five years and basic vocational schools ( *zasadnicza szkoła zawodowa* ) lasting three years. Tertiary education operates under the Bologna Process, consisting of three-year bachelor's degrees followed by two-year master's degrees, with doctoral programs typically lasting three years.
The system emphasizes foreign language proficiency, with students typically required to study two foreign languages; in 2005/06, English was the most popular, followed by German, French, and Spanish. Historical development highlights the establishment of the Jagiellonian University in 1364 and the world's first state ministry of education in 1773. Contemporary challenges include the 2017 curriculum reforms which have faced criticism for focusing excessively on nationalism and political leaders while removing references to communism and the Non-Aligned Movement. Additionally, compulsory education is enforced from age 6 to 18, though implementation has historically faced issues regarding qualified teachers and infrastructure.
